unit.title: Provide advice to executive team and stakeholders

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: The Permanent Secretary asks a director in a ministry for advice on a drought relief scheme by Friday. What should the director make clear first?
options: The decision needed, the deadline and the format
Which newspaper will report on the scheme next week
How many pages the advice must be so it looks thorough
Which officers in the ministry agree with her view

questions.stem: A director's analysis shows that a minister's favoured project is unlikely to meet its goals. What does 'frank and fearless' advice require of her?
options: Changing the analysis so that it supports the project
Saying nothing until after the project has failed
Giving the evidence honestly and respectfully
Leaking the analysis to the media to stop the project

questions.stem: The head of a housing agency is asked by a stakeholder group which political party's housing policy is better. How should she respond?
options: Give her own personal view, since the group asked her directly
Explain the agency's role and stay politically neutral
Say the governing party's policy is always better
Refuse to meet the group again in future

questions.stem: Which source is most suitable as the main evidence for advice on a youth employment programme?
options: Comments posted on a popular social media page
The view of the officer who has worked in the unit longest
A single success story reported in a newspaper
Labour force statistics and programme evaluations

questions.stem: Why should advice to an executive team usually present more than one option?
options: So the advisers can avoid blame for the final decision
So that the advice paper looks longer and more impressive
So decision makers can weigh real choices and trade-offs
So that the decision can be put off until next year

questions.stem: Option A costs J$45 million and will reach 9,000 farmers. Option B costs J$30 million and will reach 5,000 farmers. Which statement is correct?
options: Option A costs less per farmer: J$5,000 against J$6,000
Option B costs less per farmer: J$6,000 against J$5,000
Both options cost the same per farmer: J$5,500
Option B costs less per farmer: J$5,000 against J$6,000

questions.stem: The executive team meets on Monday to decide a budget item, but the full analysis will not be ready until Wednesday. What should the adviser do?
options: Send nothing and let the team decide without advice
Send the incomplete draft without saying it is a draft
Ask a colleague to guess the results for the meeting
Give interim advice and state its limits clearly

questions.stem: Before advising on a new market, a municipal corporation lists every group affected and how much each can influence the decision. What is this step called?
options: Asset depreciation
Stakeholder analysis
Cash flow forecasting
Job evaluation

questions.stem: While advice for the executive team is being prepared, a contractor asks an officer what the agency will recommend on a tender. What should the officer do?
options: Tell the contractor, since the advice will be public soon
Decline and explain that the advice is confidential
Give a hint so the contractor can prepare a better bid
Pass the question to a junior officer to answer instead

questions.stem: An adviser is asked to brief the executive team on a proposal from a firm that her brother owns. What should she do?
options: Brief the executive quickly before anyone finds out
Give advice that favours the firm, as it is a good firm
Ask her brother to write the briefing for her
Declare the conflict and step aside from the advice

questions.stem: A minister will have two minutes to read about a flood response just before a press conference. What is the best format for the advice?
options: A one-page brief with key facts and points to say
A thirty-page report with every table and appendix
A spoken message left with the minister's driver
A spreadsheet of all the raw data collected

questions.stem: Before advising the executive on changes to a school bus scheme, why should an agency consult parents, schools and bus operators?
options: So the executive can later say it never decided anything
So that the stakeholders will pay for the changes
To understand effects and raise issues before deciding
Because consultation removes all opposition at once

questions.stem: What should a piece of advice to the executive team say about risk?
options: Nothing, because risks may worry the executive team
Only the risks that would make the adviser look good
Only risks that have already happened in the past
The main risks of each option and how to manage them

questions.stem: The executive team decides against an adviser's recommendation. What should the adviser do?
options: Keep arguing at every meeting until they change course
Accept the decision and help to carry it out well
Tell stakeholders that the executive got it wrong
Slow down the work so that the decision fails

questions.stem: Why should advice given to an executive team be recorded and filed?
options: So it can be used to embarrass the executive later
So the adviser can claim credit for good results
To show what was advised, when, and on what evidence
Because every email must be printed and kept forever

questions.stem: Why must a public servant who advises a minister understand the government's stated policy priorities?
options: So advice is relevant to the decisions being made
So she can campaign for the governing party
So she can ignore evidence that conflicts with them
So she never has to give unwelcome advice

questions.stem: An adviser finds two studies with different results on the same issue. What should the advice do?
options: Report both, explain the difference and weigh them
Use only the study that suits the expected decision
Leave out both studies to keep the advice simple
Pick the study that has the most recent cover date

questions.stem: Which change would most improve a technical brief on water supply for the board of a public body?
options: Add more engineering terms to show expert knowledge
Remove all figures so that it is quicker to read
Use the longest words to sound more authoritative
Explain technical terms and lead with the main point

questions.stem: A community group expects the agency to fund its whole proposal, but the executive has approved only part of it. How should the officer handle the group?
options: Let them keep believing it will be funded in full
Tell them the executive refused out of spite
Explain the decision honestly and what is possible
Avoid the group until they finally stop asking questions

questions.stem: A stakeholder asks an adviser to promise that the executive will approve a project. What should the adviser say?
options: Promise approval, as this keeps the stakeholder happy
Explain that she advises but the executive decides
Say approval is certain if the stakeholder pays a fee
Tell the stakeholder that the project will be refused

questions.stem: What should the executive summary of an advice paper contain?
options: The history of the agency since the day it was founded
A list of everyone the adviser spoke to
The issue, the recommendation and the main reasons
The adviser's personal views on the minister

questions.stem: A serious data breach is found at an agency at 6 p.m. When should the chief executive officer be told?
options: At the next monthly management meeting
Straight away, with the facts known so far
Once the full investigation is complete
Only if the media starts asking questions

questions.stem: An adviser is comparing options for a new revenue collection system. Which set of criteria is most suitable?
options: Cost, benefit, risk, fairness and ease of delivery
The colour, size and shape of the system's screens
Which option the adviser's friends work on
Which option will take the longest to deliver

questions.stem: How can an adviser find out whether her advice is meeting the executive team's needs?
options: Assume that any silence from the team means full satisfaction
Count the total number of pages she wrote this year
Compare her advice with that of other agencies' staff
Ask the team for feedback and note how advice was used

questions.stem: Advice on a road project will also affect the water agency and the housing agency. What should the adviser do?
options: Leave their views out to keep the advice simple
Wait until those agencies complain after the decision
Ask the media what the other agencies think
Consult the other agencies and reflect their views

questions.stem: An adviser wants to include case details of named citizens in a paper for the board. What should she do first?
options: Use only what is needed, and remove names where possible
Include every personal detail so the board sees the whole story
Send the names to the board by personal email instead
Post the case details online to show transparency

questions.stem: An officer will brief the executive team in person for ten minutes. What is the best preparation?
options: Prepare to read the whole written report aloud
Prepare key points, likely questions and answers
Prepare a long list of complaints about other units
Prepare nothing, since speaking is less formal

questions.stem: Monitoring shows that a flagship programme will run J$20 million over budget. How should the director advise the executive team?
options: Hold the news until the overspend is much smaller
Tell only the finance officer and hope it is fixed
Tell them early, with causes and options to respond
Move money from other budgets without telling anyone

questions.stem: Why should an adviser state the assumptions behind a forecast in a paper to the executive team?
options: So the paper becomes much longer and looks careful
So readers can judge how reliable the forecast is
So no one can ever question the forecast again
So the executive does not need to read the figures

questions.stem: A new chief executive prefers short emailed updates, while her predecessor liked long written reports. What should the adviser do?
options: Keep sending long reports, as that is the usual way
Stop sending updates until she asks for them
Adapt to her preference, with detail on request
Send both versions every time to be safe

questions.stem: Who makes the final decision on advice given to an executive team?
options: The most junior officer who drafted the first version
The stakeholder group that speaks the most loudly
The adviser who wrote the recommendation
The executive team or office holder with authority

questions.stem: An adviser is offered an all-expenses-paid trip by a firm whose proposal she is assessing. What should she do?
options: Refuse it and report the offer under the code of conduct
Accept it, as long as she still gives fair advice afterwards
Accept it but tell no one about the trip
Accept it and give the firm a better score

questions.stem: Six months after the executive team accepted an adviser's recommendation, what is good practice?
options: Review whether the expected results are being achieved
Delete the file, since the decision has already been made
Tell stakeholders that the work is now finished
Move on to a new topic without any review of results

questions.stem: A journalist calls an adviser to ask what she told the executive team about a hospital project. What should she do?
options: Give a full account so the public is informed
Refer the call to the authorised media officer
Deny that any advice was given on the project
Share her personal view off the record

questions.stem: Farmers want water for a new irrigation scheme in one parish, while tourism operators want the same water for hotels. How should the adviser present this to the executive team?
options: Present only the farmers' view, as they asked first
Present only the hotels' view, as they earn more
Leave the conflict out so the advice looks simple
Set out both interests, the trade-offs and options

questions.stem: What makes a piece of advice 'evidence-based'?
options: It quotes the senior people who agree with the proposal
It repeats what was done in past years
It rests on sound data, research and analysis
It is written by the most senior adviser

questions.stem: A proposal will cost J$12 million in year one and save J$4 million a year from year two onward. By the end of which year will the total savings first equal the cost?
options: Year 3
Year 2
Year 4
Year 5

questions.stem: An adviser is unsure whether take-up of a new service will be 40% or 70%. What should the advice show?
options: Only the 70% case, which looks the best
Only the 40% case, which is the cautious one
An average of 55%, presented as certain
Results under both, and what changes between them

questions.stem: Why should a director build good working relationships with key stakeholders before advice is needed?
options: So stakeholders will accept any advice without question
Trust and contacts make consultation quicker and frank
So the director can share confidential papers with them
So the director can avoid using formal channels at all

questions.stem: The executive team asked for weekly updates on a hurricane recovery programme. Which update is most useful?
options: Progress against plan, issues and decisions needed
A long list of every meeting held during the week
Photographs of the staff at work with no comment
Copies of every email sent during the week

questions.stem: An adviser plans to recommend that an agency share client records with a private partner. What must she check?
options: Whether the partner's office is close to the agency
Whether the partner has a modern and well-designed website
Whether the records are stored in paper files
Whether this is lawful under the data protection law

questions.stem: Which is NOT a feature of good advice to an executive team?
options: It is timely and answers the question asked
It sets out options and their risks
It hides facts that do not fit
It is clear, accurate and well supported

questions.stem: The executive team asks an officer to represent the agency at a stakeholder forum and report back. What should the officer report?
options: The main views, any agreements and issues to decide
Only the comments that praised the agency
Only her own opinions of the people who spoke at the forum
The jokes that were made during the forum

questions.stem: The same issue must be explained to the board, to community leaders and to front-line staff. What should the adviser do?
options: Send all three groups the same technical paper
Adapt the content and format to each audience
Brief only the board and let the others hear later
Change the facts to suit what each group wants

questions.stem: After advice was sent to the executive team, the adviser finds an error in one of its figures. What should she do?
options: Tell the executive quickly and send a correction
Say nothing and hope that no one notices the error
Wait until the executive asks about the figure
Blame the clerk who typed the figures in the paper

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Complete the phrase used for honest, complete advice given even when it is unwelcome: 'frank and ____'.
Ministers are often given short suggested statements to use with the media. Complete the usual name for them: 'lines to ____'.
An option costs J$36 million and will serve 4,500 households. What is the cost per household, in J$?
What one word describes advice or information that must not be shared beyond the people entitled to see it?
What two-word term names analysis that tests how the results change when a key assumption, such as take-up, is varied?
A proposal costs J$15 million and saves J$3 million a year. What is the simple payback period in years?
What two-word name is given to a paper that sets out several possible courses of action, with the pros and cons of each, for decision makers?
An option for a municipal corporation costs J$20 million and is expected to bring benefits worth J$50 million. What is its benefit-cost ratio?
Take-up of a new service is forecast at 40% of 12,500 eligible households. How many households is this?
A survey of 800 stakeholders found that 520 supported a proposal. What percentage is this?
What one word describes advice an officer offers before being asked, for example to warn of an emerging risk?
What two-word term names the method of comparing options by giving each criterion a weight and each option a score?
Cost has a 60% weight and impact a 40% weight. Option A scores 5 for cost and 9 for impact. What is its weighted score?
Complete the term for the support and acceptance that the people affected give to a decision: 'stakeholder ____-in'.
What two-word term names the system for filing and keeping records of advice and decisions so they can be found later?

essays.stem: The executive team of a public agency asks you for advice on whether to introduce online applications for its main service. Plan how you would prepare and give the advice, from receiving the request to following it up.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first confirm the request: the decision the team must make, the deadline, the format they prefer and any limits such as budget or policy commitments. I would then gather evidence: current application numbers and costs, customer complaints, what similar agencies have done, the technology options and the legal points, such as the data protection law and the procurement rules. I would consult key stakeholders, including front-line staff, customer groups, the IT unit and finance, so that the effects on each are understood. Next I would analyse at least three options, such as staying as we are, a phased online service, or a full switch, against clear criteria: cost, benefits, risks, fairness to customers without internet access and ease of delivery. I would draft a short paper with an executive summary, the options, a clear recommendation and the main risks, and have it checked for accuracy. I would brief the team in person and answer questions honestly. After the decision, I would record the advice and decision, tell stakeholders the outcome and later review whether the expected results came.
markingPoints: Confirms the decision needed, deadline, format and limits
Gathers relevant evidence, including legal points in general terms
Consults stakeholders and analyses options against criteria
Prepares and checks a clear paper with a recommendation and risks
Briefs, records, informs stakeholders and follows up

essays.stem: Explain what 'frank and fearless' advice means for a senior public servant, and describe how to give advice that the minister or executive is unlikely to welcome.
essays.modelAnswer: Frank and fearless advice means telling decision makers the truth as the evidence shows it, including the risks and weaknesses of their preferred ideas, even when this is unwelcome. It is balanced by political neutrality and respect: the adviser gives honest advice, but the elected or appointed decision maker decides, and the adviser then carries out the decision loyally. Advice that is shaped to please, or held back, can lead to poor decisions and the waste of public money. To give unwelcome advice well, the adviser should prepare carefully, check the facts and figures, and be clear about what is known and what is uncertain. The advice should be given early, in private and through the proper channel, not through the media or stakeholders. It should acknowledge the aims behind the preferred idea and offer workable alternatives, not just objections. The tone should be calm and respectful. The advice should be put in writing and filed. If the decision goes the other way, the adviser should accept it and help to make it work, raising concerns through proper channels only where there is a legal or ethical problem.
markingPoints: Defines frank and fearless advice accurately
Links it to neutrality and the decision maker's right to decide
Explains why honest advice matters for decisions and public money
Describes preparing evidence and giving advice early, privately and respectfully, with alternatives
Records the advice and supports the final decision, using proper channels for serious concerns

essays.stem: A parish municipal corporation must choose a new garbage collection service. Option A costs J$60 million to set up and J$6 million a year to run, and will serve 10,000 households. Option B costs J$40 million to set up and J$10 million a year to run, and will serve 8,000 households. Compare the five-year cost per household, showing your working, and write the advice you would give the council's executive.
essays.modelAnswer: Over five years, Option A costs J$60 million plus 5 × J$6 million = J$30 million, a total of J$90 million. Option B costs J$40 million plus 5 × J$10 million = J$50 million, also a total of J$90 million. The totals are the same, but Option A serves more households: J$90 million ÷ 10,000 = J$9,000 per household, while Option B costs J$90 million ÷ 8,000 = J$11,250 per household. Option A therefore gives better value and reaches 2,000 more households. However, it needs J$20 million more at the start, so the council must check that the funds are available in this year's budget. My advice to the executive would be to choose Option A, because it costs less per household over five years and serves more residents. I would point out the risks: the higher upfront cost, possible delays in setting it up, and running costs rising faster than forecast. I would also advise consulting residents on collection days and following the procurement rules for public bodies when buying the service.
markingPoints: Calculates the five-year totals of J$90 million for each option
Calculates J$9,000 and J$11,250 per household
Notes the higher upfront cost of Option A and the funding check
Makes a clear, justified recommendation
Identifies risks and process points such as consultation and procurement rules

essays.stem: A municipal corporation is considering moving street vendors from a busy town centre to a new market. Plan how you would involve stakeholders while preparing advice for the executive.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by identifying the stakeholders and their interests: vendors, shop owners, shoppers, taxi and bus operators, residents, the police, the councillors and any agencies dealing with roads and health. I would rate each by how much they can influence the decision and how much it affects them, so that vendors and their associations, for example, are closely involved. I would choose methods to suit each group: meetings at the market at times vendors can attend, short surveys for shoppers, and one-to-one meetings with agencies. I would explain clearly what is being considered, what has not been decided and how views will be used, so expectations stay realistic. I would listen carefully, record views fairly, including concerns about income, transport and security, and look for ideas that could improve the plan. The advice to the executive would summarise each group's views, how the options respond to them and any remaining conflicts. After the decision, I would go back to stakeholders to explain the outcome and the reasons, and keep the lines open during the move.
markingPoints: Identifies the stakeholders and their interests
Prioritises them by influence and effect
Uses suitable methods and is clear about what is decided and what is not
Records views fairly and reflects them, including conflicts, in the advice
Reports the outcome and reasons back to stakeholders

essays.stem: Compare a written briefing paper, an oral briefing and a slide presentation as ways of giving advice to an executive team, and say when each is most suitable.
essays.modelAnswer: A written briefing paper gives a full, accurate and permanent record of the issue, options, evidence and recommendation. Readers can study it at their own pace and it can be filed as the record of advice. Its weakness is that it takes time to prepare and busy executives may not read it closely. It suits complex decisions, decisions that need a formal record and issues where figures matter. An oral briefing is quick and allows questions and discussion, so the adviser can clear up confusion at once and sense the team's concerns. However, it leaves no record unless notes are taken, and points can be forgotten. It suits urgent matters, sensitive issues best discussed in private, and updates. A slide presentation helps a group follow the main points, compare options with charts and focus discussion, but slides can oversimplify and are often not detailed enough on their own. It suits a meeting where several people must understand and discuss a proposal. In practice, the best approach often combines them: a written paper sent in advance, presented with a few slides, followed by a filed note of the decision.
markingPoints: Explains the strengths, limits and best use of a written paper
Explains the strengths, limits and best use of an oral briefing
Explains the strengths, limits and best use of a slide presentation
Mentions the need for a record of advice
Recommends combining methods where suitable

essays.stem: Explain how an adviser should protect confidential and personal information when preparing and giving advice to an executive team and stakeholders.
essays.modelAnswer: An adviser often handles sensitive information, such as draft policy, tender details, legal advice and personal data about citizens or staff. She should first know the agency's rules on classification and the general duties under the data protection law and the public service code of conduct. She should collect and use only the personal information the advice needs and remove names or identifying details where possible. Drafts should be stored on secure agency systems, not personal email or devices, with access limited to people who need it. Papers should be marked with their security level and sent only to the intended readers, and printed copies kept locked away and shredded when no longer needed. When talking with stakeholders, she must share only what is approved for release and decline politely to discuss confidential matters, referring media to the authorised spokesperson. Conversations in public places about sensitive matters should be avoided. If information is lost or leaked, she must report it at once so it can be contained. Protecting information builds trust with the executive and stakeholders and avoids legal and reputational harm.
markingPoints: Identifies the kinds of sensitive information involved
Knows the agency's rules and the general duties of the data protection law and code of conduct
Limits personal data and secures storage, marking and distribution
Shares only approved information with stakeholders and media
Reports any breach at once and explains why protection matters

essays.stem: An executive team rejects your carefully prepared recommendation and chooses another option. Explain how you should respond as a professional public servant.
essays.modelAnswer: First I should accept that the executive team has the authority to decide and that it may weigh factors beyond my analysis, such as wider policy, timing or other commitments. I should make sure my advice and the decision are both recorded, so the record shows what was advised and why the decision was made. If I believe something important was misunderstood, I may ask once, respectfully and in private, to clarify a point or a risk, but I should not keep arguing or lobby others to overturn the decision. I should then carry out the decision fully and loyally, planning how to make the chosen option work and how to manage its risks. With stakeholders and staff, I must present the decision as the agency's position and not suggest that I disagree. I should monitor the results and report them honestly, including any problems, so the team can adjust. Only if the decision were unlawful or seriously unethical would I raise the matter through the proper channels set out in the agency's rules.
markingPoints: Accepts the executive's authority to decide
Ensures advice and decision are recorded
Clarifies once, privately and respectfully, if needed, without lobbying
Implements the decision loyally and presents it as the agency's position
Monitors and reports results, using proper channels only for unlawful or unethical decisions

essays.stem: Recommend how a policy and advice unit in a ministry could evaluate and improve the quality of the advice it gives to the executive team and stakeholders.
essays.modelAnswer: I would recommend a simple quality framework with clear standards: advice should answer the question asked, arrive on time, be accurate and evidence-based, set out options and risks, be clear and concise, and consider stakeholders and the law. Each paper could be checked against these standards by a senior officer before it is sent, using a short checklist. The unit should then gather feedback from the executive team, perhaps through a short rating form after major papers and an informal review meeting every six months, asking what was useful and what was missing. It should track measures such as the share of papers delivered by the deadline, the number of corrections needed and how often advice was used in decisions. Stakeholders could be asked whether consultation was fair and whether they were told the outcome. A sample of past papers could be reviewed each year against the results of the decisions they informed. Findings should lead to action: training in writing or analysis, better templates, more time for consultation and sharing good examples across the unit.
markingPoints: Sets clear quality standards for advice
Uses a checklist or peer review before papers are sent
Gathers feedback from the executive and stakeholders
Tracks measures such as timeliness, accuracy and use
Turns findings into improvements such as training and templates

essays.stem: Heavy flooding has cut off several communities, and the executive team must decide within hours how to use emergency funds. Explain how you would give sound advice quickly when the information is incomplete.
essays.modelAnswer: In a crisis, timely advice with clear limits is better than perfect advice that comes too late. I would first agree with the executive team exactly what must be decided now and what can wait. I would gather the best information available quickly: reports from the disaster coordinators, the municipal corporations, the police and community leaders, and the funds available. I would separate confirmed facts from estimates and unknowns. I would set out two or three practical options, for example using the funds for food and water, for clearing roads, or a mix, with the main benefits, costs and risks of each. I would recommend one, explain the assumptions behind it and say what information would change the advice. The advice could be given orally, followed straight away by a short written note, so there is a record. I would set times for updates as more information comes in, and build in checks so that money is still used properly and recorded, even under pressure. After the emergency, the advice and decisions should be reviewed for lessons.
markingPoints: Agrees what must be decided now
Gathers the best available information and separates facts from estimates
Sets out a few options with benefits, costs and risks, and recommends one
States assumptions and records the advice even under pressure
Plans updates, keeps controls over funds and reviews afterwards

essays.stem: Evaluate how an adviser can manage the expectations of stakeholders who want different outcomes from the same decision, while keeping their trust.
essays.modelAnswer: Stakeholders often want different things, such as residents wanting lower fees while businesses want better services, so not everyone can get what they want. The adviser can manage this by being clear from the start about what is being decided, who decides, the timetable and the limits, such as budget and law. Honest communication matters more than promises: an adviser who suggests that everyone will be satisfied loses trust when the decision is made. Listening carefully and recording each group's views fairly shows respect, and explaining the trade-offs openly helps groups understand why their preferred outcome may not be chosen. Looking for options that meet part of each group's needs, or ways to reduce the harm to those who lose out, can reduce conflict. These approaches work best when the adviser keeps in touch throughout and reports the final decision and reasons promptly. Their limits are that some groups will still be disappointed, and an adviser cannot control the decision. Even so, a fair process, honesty and respect keep trust, so stakeholders are willing to engage again in future.
markingPoints: Recognises that stakeholder interests conflict
Is clear about scope, decision maker, timetable and limits
Communicates honestly and avoids making promises
Explains trade-offs and seeks options that reduce harm
Evaluates the limits and why a fair process keeps trust

practical1.title: Prepare a written advice paper for an executive team
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case: the executive team of a public body (for example a parish municipal corporation or a government agency) must decide how to deal with an issue, such as long queues at its main service office. The pack includes figures on demand, costs and complaints, notes from stakeholders and a short policy statement. As a group, prepare a written advice paper of three to four pages. Each member has a named role: lead adviser (confirms the question to be answered with the assessor, who plays the chief executive, and writes the executive summary and recommendation); evidence officer (summarises the data and says how reliable each source is); stakeholder analyst (maps the stakeholders by power and interest and summarises their views); options analyst (sets out at least three options and builds a spreadsheet comparing cost, cost per customer and benefits, checking every figure twice); and risk and compliance officer (lists the main risks of each option and any legal or policy points in general terms). In a group of four, the lead adviser also covers risk and compliance. Every member writes their section, and the group checks the whole paper for accuracy and clarity before handing it in.
materials: Computers with word processing and spreadsheet software
Advice paper template with executive summary, options, recommendation and risk sections
photos: The lead adviser's note of the question, deadline and format agreed with the assessor
The finished advice paper, open at the executive summary
checklist: Took a named role and completed their section
The paper answers the question asked and leads with a clear recommendation
Evidence is summarised accurately and its reliability is stated
At least three options are compared against clear criteria, with correct figures checked twice
Risks and legal or policy points are covered in general terms
The writing is clear, concise and professional
safety: Treat the case pack and stakeholder notes as confidential; return them to the assessor
Use made-up names only and no real personal data
Share the workload fairly and take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Brief an executive team and report back to stakeholders
practical2.brief: Using a made-up case from the assessor (for example a public agency deciding whether to change its opening hours, with a one-page advice note), your group runs two short role plays and produces records of each. Part A (30 minutes): the oral briefing. The lead adviser briefs the executive team for 10 minutes, using no more than four slides or a one-page handout, and answers questions; two members play executive team members who ask probing questions from a card given by the assessor; the note-taker records the questions, answers and the decision. Part B (30 minutes): the stakeholder meeting. The stakeholder liaison officer explains the decision to a stakeholder group (two members play community and business representatives with role cards) and handles their concerns; the note-taker records the meeting. Part C (45 minutes): the group writes a file note of the advice and decision, notes of the stakeholder meeting with actions, and a short letter to stakeholders confirming the decision and the next steps. Members swap so that every member speaks in at least one role play and writes at least one document. In a group of four, one executive team member also plays a stakeholder.
materials: Case pack, advice note and role cards from the assessor
Computer and screen, or printed handouts
File note, meeting notes and letter templates
A table set up for each meeting
photos: The oral briefing in progress (faces only if all agree)
The note-taker's record of questions and the decision
The stakeholder meeting in progress (faces only if all agree)
The file note, the meeting notes and the letter to stakeholders
checklist: Took the agreed roles and took part in at least one role play
The briefing leads with the main point, gives options and risks, and stays within time
Questions were answered honestly, including what is not known
The decision was explained to stakeholders clearly, without blaming the executive or making promises
Concerns were listened to and recorded fairly, with actions
The file note and letter are accurate, clear and professional
safety: Keep the role cards and notes confidential; return them to the assessor
Keep the role play respectful: challenge ideas, not people
Stay politically neutral and use made-up names only
Take a short break between parts and share the writing fairly
